performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: The second movement, “Il vecchio castello” (Andante), depicts a troubadour singing outside a medieval castle. In Ravel’s orchestration an alto saxophone plays the song over a repeated G♯.

sections.label: A · Song over the G♯ drone
sections.mNote: Bassoon and alto saxophone play the castle’s song.

sections.label: B · D major above a G♯ drone
sections.mNote: The chords change over a held G♯ in the bass.

sections.label: C · Chromatic turns above G♯ pedal
sections.mNote: The melody climbs by semitones over the repeated bass.

sections.label: Coda · Last statement of the song over G♯
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns, then breaks into short phrases.

cues.title: Pedal G♯ in 6/8
cues.text: The bass repeats G♯ throughout, in a rocking 6/8. Above it the bassoon opens the movement, and the alto saxophone plays the long melody, whose phrases range high above the held bass note.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano text, Il vecchio castello, establishes the repeated G♯ and 6/8. Bassoon and saxophone roles are described in the movement commentary at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictures_at_an_Exhibition ; Ravel’s scoring is inferred for this recording. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/il-vecchio-castello.ly
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Troubadour before a medieval castle
cues.text: Hartmann travelled in Italy and painted its buildings. Mussorgsky placed a singer, a troubadour, in front of a medieval castle, and the long melody is his song. The particular picture has not been identified.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note quotes Stasov’s description of the troubadour and connects the movement with Hartmann’s Italian architectural watercolours. The particular picture is unidentified. https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: D major over the G♯ pedal
cues.text: The tune expands into octaves and chords. At bars 31 and 40 a chord of D major sounds above the G♯ bass, so that its D lies a tritone from the note below. The G♯ pedal stays unchanged under every change of harmony.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano text, Il vecchio castello, bars 29–46; D-major chords appear at bars 31 and 40 over the unchanged G♯ pedal. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/il-vecchio-castello.ly
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel’s orchestration, 1922
cues.text: In the summer of 1922 Ravel orchestrated Pictures for Serge Koussevitzky. He gave the medieval singer’s melody to the alto saxophone. Koussevitzky conducted the first performance of the new score in Paris that October.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note gives the 1922 commission, summer orchestration, October Paris première and alto saxophone solo. https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: Return of the opening melody
cues.text: The opening melody returns near the end and is broken into short phrases separated by rests. G♯ continues underneath. A final upward phrase reaches the upper G♯ in bar 106, and the bass ends on G♯ in bar 107.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano text, Il vecchio castello, bars 95–107: returning melody, rests, final upper G♯ at bar 106 and bass G♯ at bar 107. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/il-vecchio-castello.ly
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: New chords over the same bass
transitions.from: A · Song over the G♯ drone
transitions.to: B · D major above a G♯ drone
transitions.how: The repeated G♯ continues as a pedal through bars 29–46, beneath a melody now played in octaves. A-major and D-major chords pass above it, and their notes are dissonant against the bass. The lowest part keeps the same rocking rhythm on G♯ while the harmony above it changes.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano text, Il vecchio castello, bars 29–46: upper octaves and A- and D-major chords above the G♯ pedal. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/il-vecchio-castello.ly

transitions.title: The first song returns over G♯
transitions.from: C · Chromatic turns above G♯ pedal
transitions.to: Coda · Last statement of the song over G♯
transitions.how: The opening song returns in G♯ minor, marked espressivo, over the same G♯ bass. Its long line breaks up into separate chords divided by rests. The last upward leap of the melody reaches G♯, and the bass goes on for a short time below it.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano text, Il vecchio castello, bars 95–107. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/il-vecchio-castello.ly

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (4:46; this file is 4:44), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
